## NGO Website Development in India: Building a Donor Wall and Supporter Recognition Page Without Exposing Donor Data

An NGO website can thank donors publicly, through a donor wall, a "supporters" page or a list of corporate partners, as long as it asks each donor for explicit, specific permission first, shows only what they agreed to, and lets them change their mind. Treat recognition as an opt-in feature with its own checkbox on the donation form, not as something that follows automatically from a payment. That one design decision decides whether a donor wall builds trust or creates a complaint.

This guide is for Indian NGO founders, fundraising heads and the people who manage their websites. It explains why donor recognition is worth doing, which kinds of recognition suit which donors, what to collect and what to leave out, how the data protection rules shape the design, how to build the page so it is fast and accessible, and how to run it day to day. Where we mention law, we describe the general direction and tell you what to verify with your own adviser. We have not invented donation figures or examples. The worked example is hypothetical and labelled as such.

### Why a donor wall is worth building, and when it is not

Public thanks does three things for a small NGO:

- It shows new visitors that real people and organisations stand behind the work, which supports trust at the moment someone is deciding whether to give.
- It makes existing donors feel seen, which helps retention. Our guide to [donor retention automation](/blog/donor-retention-automation-ngos/) explains why the first thank-you and second gift matter so much.
- It gives corporate and CSR partners visible credit, which they often expect. See our article on [qualifying for CSR funding](/blog/qualify-csr-funding-india/).

It is not worth doing when:

- Most of your supporters give small sums and prefer privacy, for example for sensitive causes such as health, domestic violence or addiction.
- You do not have the staff to review and maintain the list.
- The cause could expose donors to risk if their names were public.

In those cases, a message such as "Thank you to the many people who give quietly" and aggregate impact figures may be a better form of recognition.

## Types of recognition, from least to most exposed

Pick the lightest option that meets the goal.

| Type | What appears | Privacy risk | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aggregate thanks | "Supported by donors across 20 cities" (only if true) | Very low | Sensitive causes, small donors |
| First name and city | "Anita, Pune" | Low to medium | Community campaigns |
| Full name | "Anita Kulkarni" | Medium | Donors who ask to be named |
| Named tribute or dedication | "In memory of …" | Medium, involves a third person | Memorial gifts. See our [tribute and gift donation guide](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-tribute-in-memory-gift-donations-dedication-forms-2026/) |
| Organisation logo and link | A company or trust logo | Low, business information | CSR and corporate partners |
| Amount band | "Silver supporter" | Medium | Tiered programmes only if donors choose it |

Avoid showing exact amounts unless the donor explicitly wants them shown. Amounts can expose a person's finances and, on a public list, can create pressure on other donors.

## What to ask the donor, and when

### Put it on the donation form, not in the fine print

Add one unticked checkbox near the end of the form: "Show my name on the supporters page." Then, if ticked, reveal a small set of controls:

- **Display name.** A text field pre-filled from the donor's name that they can change to a first name, initials or a business name. Do not force the legal name.
- **Display location.** Optional, with city only. Do not display full addresses.
- **Message.** Optional short message, moderated before publishing.
- **Amount visibility.** Default off.

Keep the receipt details separate from the display details. The name on a tax receipt must match the donor's records, but the name on the wall can differ. Our guide to [donation page design](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donation-page-design-2026/) shows where optional fields fit without lowering completion.

### Never pre-tick the box

A pre-ticked box is not meaningful permission. Under India's data protection rules, consent is meant to be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, and to be given by a clear affirmative action. Pre-ticked recognition fails the plain-language version of that test.

### Make it separate from the gift

A donor should be able to give without agreeing to recognition. Do not make the checkbox mandatory, and do not offer a reward that effectively pushes people into it.

### Confirm by email or WhatsApp

After the donation, send a short message: "You asked us to list 'Anita, Pune' on our supporters page. Reply STOP or click here to remove it any time." This gives donors a second look at what will be shown, and it creates a record that they confirmed. If you use WhatsApp for donor messages, follow the opt-in practices in [WhatsApp opt-in compliance](/blog/whatsapp-opt-in-compliance-checklist/).

## The data protection angle

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the Rules notified in November 2025 are being brought into force in stages, with the main obligations for data fiduciaries expected to apply from around May 2027 according to published commentary. Our explainers on [donor data protection under the DPDP Act](/blog/ngo-donor-data-protection-dpdp-act-2026/) and [DPDP compliance for websites](/blog/dpdp-act-website-compliance-india-2026/) describe the general direction. Verify the exact dates and your obligations with a qualified adviser. This article is not legal advice.

For a donor wall, the principles translate into a few design rules:

1. **Purpose limitation.** Data given for a receipt should not quietly be reused for public display. Ask for display consent separately.
2. **Notice.** Say plainly, next to the checkbox, what will be shown, where, and for how long.
3. **Withdrawal.** Make it as easy to remove a name as it was to add it. A "Remove my name" link in every confirmation message, handled within a stated time, is a good practice.
4. **Data minimisation.** Collect and show the minimum. A first name and city is usually enough.
5. **Children.** If a donor may be under 18, for example a school fundraiser, talk to your adviser about what the rules require before publishing any child's details.
6. **Third parties.** For tributes, you may be publishing the name of someone who has died, or of a living person who has not agreed. Decide your policy and apply it consistently.

Separately, the tax and regulatory side, such as 80G receipts and FCRA reporting for foreign contributions, does not require you to publish donors. Do not confuse regulatory reporting, which goes to authorities, with public recognition, which is voluntary. Our [NGO donation transparency checklist](/blog/ngo-donation-transparency-checklist/) explains what you should publish about your finances and what you should not.

## Foreign donors and sensitive cases

If you accept foreign contributions under FCRA, take extra care. A public list that includes foreign donors, or that sits beside content about politically sensitive work, may have consequences for the donor that you cannot foresee. Our guide on [tracking domestic and foreign donations](/blog/domestic-foreign-donation-tracking/) covers the record-keeping side. For the display side, the safest default is to avoid listing foreign individuals publicly unless they ask and your adviser agrees.

For causes where publicity could expose a donor to risk, offer anonymous giving as the default and a clear statement that you do not publish names.

## Corporate and CSR partner recognition

Companies usually want their logo and a link, and sometimes a line describing the programme they funded. This is a business relationship, so handle it through an agreement.

- Get written permission to use the logo and name, and agree where and for how long it will appear.
- Use the logo files the company supplies, at the sizes they allow.
- Describe the funded programme accurately. Do not imply an endorsement that the partner has not given.
- Keep partner pages consistent: logo, name, programme, year.
- Remove the partner when the agreement ends or the company asks.

Ensure the page does not look like a paid advertising section, because that can confuse regulators and donors. For reporting to CSR partners, see [CSR grant reporting](/blog/csr-grant-reporting-checklist/).

## Building the page

### Data model

Store recognition data separately from the donation record. A simple structure is:

- A `recognition` record linked to a donor ID, with the fields: display name, display city, message, amount visibility, consent timestamp, consent wording version, status (pending, approved, withdrawn).
- A separate public view that returns only approved records and only the display fields.

This separation means the public page can never accidentally expose email, phone, PAN or address, because those fields do not exist in the public data source. Keep the donor's private details out of any JSON that the browser can read.

### Moderation

Approve entries before they appear. Review names and messages for abuse, impersonation and commercial spam. A donor could type another person's name, a slogan or a link. Strip links from messages and set a length limit. Keep a log of who approved what.

### Display

- Show names as plain text in a simple grid or list. A scrolling ticker is hard to read and hard to pause, which is an accessibility problem.
- Paginate or load in batches if the list is long, so the page stays light. Large lists make slow pages, which hurts both users and search. See our guide on [store speed and Core Web Vitals](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-store-speed-core-web-vitals-2026/), which applies equally to a donation site.
- Use sufficient colour contrast and real HTML text. See [accessibility and donor trust](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-accessibility-donor-trust-2026/).
- Offer a short "How we thank donors and how to be removed" note at the top of the page.

### Search engines and privacy

A public list of names will be indexed by search engines. That means a donor's name, plus city, can appear in search results for their name. Make sure donors know this when they agree. If you want to reduce the effect, use first names and initials, or add a `noindex` tag to the supporters page. A `noindex` page does not give privacy by itself, because the page is still public to anyone with the link. Choose the option that matches what you told donors.

When a donor withdraws, remove the entry from the page and from the data, and be aware that search engines and archives may keep copies for a time. Tell donors this honestly.

### Sharing and social previews

If you want donors to share their recognition on WhatsApp or social media, set up preview images and descriptions carefully. Our article on [WhatsApp and social share previews](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-whatsapp-social-share-previews-open-graph-campaigns-2026/) covers the Open Graph tags that control what appears.

## A hypothetical example

Consider a fictional small trust running a scholarship fund, which we will call Example Trust. It is not a real client.

- The donation form has an unticked box, "Show my name on our supporters page", and a note explaining that the name will be public and can be removed at any time.
- Only first name and city are shown by default. A donor can type a different display name.
- An administrator approves each entry. Messages are limited to 140 characters, with links removed.
- Two weeks after a donation, the donor receives a message with a "Remove my name" link.
- Corporate partners appear in a separate "Programme partners" section, based on signed agreements.
- The public page loads from a view that has no email, phone, PAN or amount data in it.

Nothing about this is complicated. The effort goes into the consent wording and the habit of honouring removal requests quickly.

## Running it after launch

A donor wall needs light, regular care.

- **Weekly.** Approve new entries and process removal requests.
- **Monthly.** Check the page for broken images, outdated partner logos and entries that donors have asked to change.
- **Yearly.** Review the policy and wording, and refresh partner agreements. Delete old data you no longer need.
- **When something goes wrong.** If a name is shown by mistake, remove it at once, tell the person, and record what happened. Our [CMS roles guide](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-cms-roles-staff-updates-2026/) explains how to limit who can publish entries.

Measure whether it helps. In your analytics, compare conversion rates on the donation page before and after adding the recognition option, and track the share of donors who opt in. Use GA4 events as described in [donation analytics and the GA4 funnel](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donation-analytics-ga4-funnel-2026/). If few donors opt in, that is information, not failure. Many people prefer privacy.

## Common mistakes

- Publishing every donor by default.
- Showing exact amounts.
- Displaying full addresses or phone numbers.
- Using a scrolling ticker that cannot be paused.
- Letting volunteers edit the list with no approval step.
- Leaving removed donors visible on cached pages or old social posts.
- Mixing foreign donors into a public list without advice.
- Treating a donor wall as a substitute for transparent financial reporting. Donors want to see where money went, not only who gave it.

## Where to start

1. Decide whether recognition suits your cause and donors.
2. Choose the lightest recognition type that serves the goal.
3. Add an unticked opt-in checkbox and a clear notice to the donation form.
4. Separate the recognition data from the donation record.
5. Build an approval and removal process.
6. Draft the privacy wording with your adviser.
7. Launch to a small group of supporters and ask for feedback.

If you would like help with this, see our [NGO website development page](/pages/ngopage/). Pricing is confirmed by the team on WhatsApp. You may also like to read about [website creation](/services/website-creation/) and [our payment gateway integration](/services/payment-gateway/) services.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can an NGO publish its donors' names on its website?

Only with the donor's clear permission for that specific purpose. Ask through an unticked checkbox on the donation form, show only what the donor agreed to, and give an easy way to withdraw. Being legally allowed to hold a donor's data for receipts does not by itself give you permission to display it.

### Should a donor wall show donation amounts?

Usually not. Amounts reveal personal finances and can pressure other donors. Show amounts only if the donor specifically chooses to share them, and consider tier labels instead.

### How do I handle a donor who asks to be removed?

Remove the entry from the public page and from the recognition data promptly, confirm to the donor in writing, and keep a short internal record. Explain that search engines and archives may take time to drop cached copies.

### Do 80G receipts or FCRA reports require a public donor list?

No. Receipts and statutory reports serve your records and the authorities. Public recognition is a separate, voluntary choice that needs the donor's agreement.

### How do I thank corporate CSR partners on the website?

Agree it in writing, use the logo the company supplies, describe the funded programme accurately, and set a start and end for the display. Keep it factual so it does not read as advertising.


For showing campaign totals as well as thanking donors, see [building honest fundraising progress bars](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-fundraising-progress-bar-goal-thermometer-2026).

## Sources

- Press Information Bureau, Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 (notification), and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, for the consent and withdrawal principles.
- Deccan Herald and other published commentary on the phased implementation of the Rules, for the general timeline of 12 to 18 months from November 2025. Confirm exact dates against the official text.
- Google Search Central documentation on the `noindex` directive.
